title: Bit Manipulation [Concepts & Problems]
tagline: light switches inside the machine — eight tiny doors per byte

placementQuiz.q: XOR of a bit with itself is…
placementQuiz.explain: Same cancels same — magic property later.

blocks.md: **Every number is a row of on/off switches. Bits give you direct hands on those switches.**
Row above reads 00001011 → 8+2+1 = **11**. Position i carries value 2^i. That's all binary is.

items: **<<** shift left = ×2 per step · **>>** shift right = ÷2 per step (floor)

blocks.label: parity + doubling in the wild
blocks.code:
if (x & 1) cout << "odd";      // last switch ON
x << 1;                        // double
x >> 1;                        // halve (floor)
bool kthOn = (x >> k) & 1;     // read door k
x = x | (1 << k);              // turn ON
x = x & ~(1 << k);             // turn OFF
x = x ^ (1 << k);              // FLIP door k

items.title: Even/Odd via Bitwise
hints: Negative numbers: still works for parity on two's complement.

solutionCode.label: the lowest bit IS the parity
solutionCode.py:
def is_odd(x: int) -> bool:
    return (x & 1) != 0


def is_even(x: int) -> bool:
    return (x & 1) == 0
# TRUTH TABLE: any binary number ends in 0 (even) or 1 (odd). ANDing with 1
# keeps only that bit. Two's complement means -7 & 1 == 1, still correctly odd --
# unlike C++'s -7 % 2 == -1, which breaks a naive "== 1" parity test.

items.complexity: O(1) — a single AND instruction, typically faster than the modulo it replaces.

followups.q: Why does this beat x % 2 for parity?
followups.a: In C++ the modulo of a negative number is negative, so -7 % 2 is -1 and a test for == 1 silently fails. AND with 1 reads the actual sign-bit-independent last bit, giving 1 for every odd number regardless of sign. It also compiles to one instruction rather than a division.

followups.q: Does it work in Python too?
followups.a: Yes, and Python's % happens to agree here because Python floors toward negative infinity, making -7 % 2 == 1. The AND is still preferable as a portable idiom — it means the same thing in every language, which the modulo does not.

items.title: Print Binary Representation
items.statement: Build bit string MSB→LSB using shifts/mask loop.
hints: Loop from high bit down, test (n>>i)&1.
Or build reversed then reverse string.

solutionCode.label: walk from the high bit down, testing one bit at a time

items.complexity: O(width) — 32 iterations for a 32-bit integer, so effectively O(1).

followups.q: Why walk downward rather than upward?
followups.a: Written binary is most-significant first, and shifting right by i then masking extracts bit i. Starting at 31 and descending emits them in written order directly. Walking upward gives the reversed string, which then needs an extra reversal pass — the same choice as the stack version in the queues module.

followups.q: Why mask with 0xFFFFFFFF in Python?
followups.a: Python integers are arbitrary precision and negatives have infinitely many leading 1s conceptually, so -1 >> 31 is still -1. Masking to 32 bits gives the two's-complement byte pattern a C++ int would hold, which is what "print the binary representation" means for a fixed-width type.

items.title: Get / Set / Clear / Toggle Kth Bit

solutionCode.label: one mask, four operations

followups.q: Why does XOR toggle rather than set?
followups.a: XOR with 1 flips a bit (0^1=1, 1^1=0) while XOR with 0 leaves it alone. The mask has a single 1 at position k, so exactly that bit flips and every other bit XORs with 0 and survives. OR can only turn bits on; AND can only turn them off; XOR is the only one that inverts.

followups.q: Why does updateBit clear before OR-ing?
followups.a: If the bit is already 1 and value is 0, a plain OR cannot turn it off. Clearing first guarantees a known 0, then the OR writes the desired value. Doing it in one expression avoids a branch, which matters in tight loops where the value is data-dependent.

items.title: Count Set Bits (loop version)
items.statement: Count ON switches by walking bits.

solutionCode.label: shift and test, one bit position at a time
solutionCode.py:
def count_set_bits(n: int) -> int:
    n &= 0xFFFFFFFF               # treat as unsigned 32-bit, like the C++ version
    count = 0
    while n:
        count += n & 1
        n >>= 1
    return count
# SIGNED TRAP: in C++ a signed -1 >> 1 stays -1 (arithmetic shift preserves the
# sign bit), so the same loop never terminates. Masking to unsigned avoids it.

items.complexity: O(width) — one iteration per bit position, 32 for an int. Kernighan (X202) does one per SET bit instead.

followups.q: Why must n be unsigned?
followups.a: Right-shifting a negative signed integer is an arithmetic shift on virtually every compiler: the sign bit is replicated, so -1 >> 1 is still -1 and the loop never reaches zero. Unsigned uses a logical shift that feeds in zeros, guaranteeing termination in at most 32 steps.

followups.q: How does this compare to Kernighan?
followups.a: This runs once per bit POSITION — always 32 iterations for an int. Kernighan's n &= n-1 runs once per SET bit, so counting the bits of 8 (one bit set) takes one iteration instead of 32. Same worst case, much better on sparse values.

items.title: Is Power of Two (divide walk)
items.statement: Naive: keep dividing by 2; watch n=0 trap.

solutionCode.label: divide-walk version, with the n <= 0 trap handled first

items.complexity: O(log n) — one halving per iteration.

followups.q: Why exactly does n = 0 break the naive version without the guard?
followups.a: 0 % 2 is 0, so the loop condition holds, but 0 / 2 is 0 — the value never changes and the loop spins forever. Even if you wrote it as a for-loop that terminates, the final test would be 0 == 1, false, only by accident. The guard makes the intent explicit rather than relying on a coincidence.

followups.q: What is the one-line version?
followups.a: n > 0 && (n & (n-1)) == 0. Subtracting 1 from a power of two flips its single set bit to 0 and all lower bits to 1, so the AND is zero. X203 covers it — but the divide-walk is worth writing first to see WHY the bit trick works.

items.title: Swap Two Numbers Without Temp (XOR)
hints: Caveat aloud: same-variable call self-zeros (UB territory).

solutionCode.label: three XORs, with the aliasing caveat stated
solutionCode.py:
def xor_swap(a: int, b: int) -> tuple:
    """Returns (b, a) using only XOR. TRACE with a=5 (0101), b=9 (1001):
         a ^= b  ->  1100 (12)
         b ^= a  ->  0101 (5)   b now holds the original a
         a ^= b  ->  1001 (9)   a now holds the original b

    CAVEAT: applied to the SAME storage location (aliasing), this zeros it --
    x ^= x is 0. In C++ that means guarding &a == &b before swapping."""
    a ^= b
    b ^= a
    a ^= b
    return a, b

items.complexity: O(1), three XOR operations, no temporary variable.

followups.q: What goes wrong when both arguments are the same variable?
followups.a: The first XOR computes x ^ x, which is 0, destroying the value before the other two lines can recover it — the variable ends up 0 instead of unchanged. std::swap has no such hazard, which is one reason the XOR trick is a curiosity rather than a recommendation.

followups.q: Is XOR swap actually faster?
followups.a: No. Modern compilers implement a three-move swap using registers, often eliminating it entirely through register renaming, while the XOR version creates a serial dependency chain that defeats instruction-level parallelism. It saves a register on 1970s hardware; today it is slower and riskier.

items.title: Check If Kth Bit Set (GFG style)

solutionCode.label: shift the number down, or shift the mask up
solutionCode.py:
def is_kth_bit_set_a(n: int, k: int) -> bool:
    """STYLE A -- shift the NUMBER right, then read bit 0."""
    return ((n >> k) & 1) != 0


def is_kth_bit_set_b(n: int, k: int) -> bool:
    """STYLE B -- shift the MASK left, then test with AND."""
    return (n & (1 << k)) != 0
# Equivalent for k in range. In C++ both are undefined behaviour when k is at
# or beyond the type's bit width; Python has no such limit.

followups.q: Are the two styles ever different?
followups.a: For valid k they are equivalent. They diverge on overflow: in C++, 1 << 31 on a signed int is undefined behaviour, so style B needs 1u << 31. Style A shifts the value instead of the mask, sidestepping that particular problem but introducing the arithmetic-shift issue for negative n.

followups.q: What happens when k exceeds the bit width?
followups.a: Undefined behaviour in C and C++ — not "returns zero". On x86 the shift amount is taken modulo 32, so 1 << 32 gives 1, silently wrong. Python simply returns 0 for the AND since integers are unbounded. Always bound-check k when it comes from input.

items.title: Multiply/Divide by 2^k via Shifts
items.statement: Implement mulPow2/divPow2 helpers; note negative right-shift floors toward −∞.

solutionCode.label: shifts are power-of-two arithmetic, with the negative-division caveat
solutionCode.py:
def mul_pow2(n: int, k: int) -> int:
    return n << k                 # n * 2^k


def div_pow2(n: int, k: int) -> int:
    return n >> k                 # FLOOR division by 2^k
# NEGATIVE CAVEAT: right shift floors toward negative infinity.
#   -7 >> 1 == -4  (floor of -3.5)
#   int(-7 / 2) == -3  (truncation toward zero)
# Python's // also floors, so -7 // 2 == -4 and agrees with the shift --
# but C++'s / truncates, so there the two differ.

items.complexity: O(1) — a single shift instruction each.

followups.q: When is x >> 1 NOT the same as x / 2?
followups.a: Whenever x is negative and odd. The shift floors (-7 >> 1 is -4) while C++ integer division truncates toward zero (-7 / 2 is -3). Compilers therefore cannot blindly replace division by a shift for signed types — they emit extra correction instructions, which is why unsigned division by a constant is genuinely faster.

followups.q: What is the overflow risk with the left shift?
followups.a: Shifting a 1 bit into or past the sign position is undefined behaviour for signed types in C++. 1 << 31 on a signed int is already UB, and n << k silently discards the high bits when the result exceeds the width. Python has no width, so it just grows the integer — a real semantic difference between the two implementations.

items.title: Highest Set Bit Position
hints: Or loop from top bit downward first-hit.

solutionCode.label: shift right counting until the value vanishes

items.complexity: O(log n) with the shift-count loop; O(1) with a hardware intrinsic.

followups.q: Why is the answer floor(log2(n))?
followups.a: The most significant set bit at position p means the value is at least 2^p and less than 2^(p+1), so log2(n) lies in [p, p+1) and its floor is p. That is why this function is the integer log — and why it is the standard way to size a sparse table or find a binary-lifting bound.

followups.q: Why does n = 0 need special handling in the fast version?
followups.a: __builtin_clz is undefined for zero — it does not return 32, it returns garbage or traps depending on the CPU. Python's bit_length() returns 0 for zero, which would give -1 through the subtraction, but the explicit guard documents the intent rather than relying on that.

items.title: Binary Gap
items.statement: Longest run of zeros between two 1s.

solutionCode.label: remember the position of the last 1 seen

items.complexity: O(width) — one pass over the bits.

followups.q: Why does tracking the last 1 handle leading and trailing zeros for free?
followups.a: The gap is only measured between two set bits, and lastOne is only assigned when a 1 is found. Zeros before the first 1 never trigger a measurement because lastOne is still -1, and zeros after the final 1 never trigger one because no further 1 arrives. No explicit trimming is needed.

followups.q: What is the answer for a single set bit?
followups.a: Zero — LeetCode 868 defines the distance as requiring two adjacent 1s, and with only one there is no pair. The same applies to n = 0. Both fall out of initialising best to 0 and never entering the measurement branch.
